title: Phonon-limited detection thresholds for genetically encoded fluorescent-protein spin-qubit relaxometry of neural radicals
authors: Parul Raghuvanshi, Sagnik Ganguly, Sharika E, Mohana Priya T., Vishvendra S. Poonia
abstract: The demonstration that enhanced yellow fluorescent protein hosts an optically addressable spin-1 qubit in its metastable triplet state raises the prospect of genetically encoded quantum sensing at molecular length scales. We develop a detection-limit theory for using this fluorescent-protein spin qubit (FPSQ) to sense paramagnetic neural signaling radicals by spin relaxometry. We derive the transition-resolved Redfield relaxation matrix of the zero-field-split triplet coupled to a diffusing radical bath, establish the regime in which it collapses to a single exponential, and validate it against Lindblad simulations and nitrogen-vacancy benchmarks. Propagating the effects of photon shot noise, photobleaching-grounded photon budget, and finite measurement bandwidth, we find that the native room-temperature sensor falls short of physiological sensitivity by six to eight orders of magnitude with the bottleneck being the phonon-limited intrinsic $\Tone$. Analyzing the underlying direct and two-phonon Raman processes, we show that room-temperature relaxation is Raman-dominated by $\sim\!720\!:\!1$ and that, because the Raman coefficient scales as $v^{-10}$ with sound velocity, a $\sim\!2\times$ stiffening of the chromophore environment recovers $\Tone\sim\SI{100}{\micro\second}$, sufficient for micromolar sensing. Nanomolar sensing is obstructed by a direct-process ceiling of \SI{79}{\micro\second} that vibronic decoupling alone cannot breach. We obtain quantitative design rules, identify photon yield as a co-equal bottleneck, and propose a frequency-resolved protocol for chemical specificity.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to determine the sensitivity limit of using a fluorescent protein as a spin-1 qubit to detect neural radicals. The analysis shows that the sensor's performance is fundamentally limited by its own intrinsic, phonon-mediated relaxation rate. By modeling the relaxation dynamics and proposing environmental stiffening, the authors provide concrete pathways to improve the qubit's coherence time for practical biological sensing.
main_problem: To develop a detection-limit theory for using a fluorescent-protein spin-qubit (FPSQ) to sense paramagnetic neural signaling radicals via spin relaxometry.
main_result: The native room-temperature sensor is limited by its intrinsic, phonon-limited T1, falling short of physiological sensitivity by 6 to 8 orders of magnitude. Improving the chromophore environment stiffness by 2x is predicted to recover T1 sufficient for micromolar sensing.
method: The authors derived a transition-resolved Redfield relaxation matrix for the spin-1 qubit coupled to a diffusing radical bath, analyzing the resulting relaxation dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is an enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (EYFP) acting as an optically addressable spin-1 qubit in its metastable triplet state. Sensing occurs via spin relaxometry, where the radical's fluctuating field shortens the qubit's longitudinal relaxation time (T1).
key_observables: Longitudinal relaxation time (T1), relaxivity ($\kappa$), and the effective relaxation rate ($\Gamma_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Phonon-limited intrinsic T1, correlation time ($	au_c$), and the ratio of Raman to direct relaxation processes ($\sim 720:1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the noise spectrum is Lorentzian and that the system can be treated in the single-exponential decay limit for fast radicals.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes mention comparisons to Lindblad simulations and Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) benchmarks.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical platform (FPSQ), develops the theoretical framework (Redfield theory for spin relaxation), analyzes the limiting factors (phonon-limited T1), and proposes design rules for improvement.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced open quantum system theory (Redfield/Lindblad) to a solid-state, bio-molecular quantum sensor, providing quantitative design rules for enhancing coherence times in a complex, noisy environment.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Proposed FPSQ relaxometry concept. (a) A genetically anchored fluorescent protein spin qubit (FPSQ) is placed close to a radical-producing enzyme and read out optically at 912 nm. (b) The EYFP triplet acts as a spin-1 qubit with three zero-field ODMR transitions at 2E, D −E, and D + E. (c) A fluctuating radical bath adds a longitudinal relaxation channel, ∆Γ1 = κn, which shortens the triplet polarization decay measured after a dark time τ. This change is used to estimate the local radical density.

(a) Population transfer rates for the three zero-field transitions, each driven by an orthogonal component of the dipolar field noise sampled at its own frequency ωij.
